about.title: About
about.desc: What Relire Plus is and where your data goes.
about.what: Relire Plus is a close-reading assistant for French learners preparing for TCF Canada. Read real articles, open any word or sentence for an explanation, and practise saying them aloud.
about.privacy: There is no account and no app server. Your articles, vocabulary and recordings stay in this browser. When you use an AI feature, the text or recording goes straight from this browser to the provider you chose, with your own key.
about.servicePrivacy: This version can read grammar topics, a complete paged wordbook and additional graded readers from a content service. Requests carry a topic id, book id/page/version, or published reader id/version, with your IP address like any web request. It never receives your articles, contexts, answers, ratings, schedules or recordings, and never an AI provider key: the only key it receives is the access key you set for it. Wordbook download exposes the whole published book to clients.
about.scope: Relire Plus is a study aid. It has no mock exams and gives no official scores, and AI feedback is an estimate.
about.lexicon: The word sheet’s verb forms and tenses come from {{name}}, maintained by {{maintainer}} and licensed {{licence}}: a dictionary that ships with the app and needs no service.
about.lexiconRebuild: The dictionary data ships with the app as a generated file.

notes.ou: Sounds approximately like the ‘ou’ in English ‘soup’: round your lips and keep the vowel steady.
notes.oi: Read like 'wa', smoothly gliding from a w sound into an open a.
notes.au: au usually makes one steady rounded ‘o’ sound; do not glide into a second vowel as in English ‘boat’.
notes.eau: eau makes the same steady rounded ‘o’ sound as au, without an English-style vowel glide.
notes.eu: When no consonant sound follows eu in its syllable, it usually has this steady vowel: round your lips and keep your tongue forward.
notes.on: on usually makes this nasal vowel when the next letter in the same word is neither a vowel nor n or m, or when the word ends: let air flow through both mouth and nose, without adding an n sound.
notes.an: an usually makes a nasal vowel, roughly a nasalized ‘ah’, when the next letter in the same word is neither a vowel nor n or m, or when the word ends; air flows through both mouth and nose.
notes.en: en usually makes the same nasal vowel as an when the next letter in the same word is neither a vowel nor n or m, or when the word ends; air flows through both mouth and nose.
notes.in: in usually makes this nasal vowel when the next letter in the same word is neither a vowel nor n or m, or when the word ends: let air flow through both mouth and nose, without adding an n sound.
notes.ain: ain usually makes the same nasal vowel as in when the next letter in the same word is neither a vowel nor n or m, or when the word ends; air flows through both mouth and nose, with no added n sound.
notes.ch: Pronounced like the 'sh' in English 'shoe', produced with air flowing gently over the tongue.
notes.gn: Usually one n-like sound made with the tongue against the hard palate, roughly like ‘ny’ in English ‘canyon’ but without separating n and y.
notes.qu: qu usually sounds like the k in English ‘key’; in these words, u has no separate sound.
notes.c-cedille: ç sounds like the s in English ‘see’ and is used before a, o or u.
notes.ph: Pronounced like the 'f' in English 'fish', with the upper teeth lightly resting on the lower lip.
notes.h: It is never pronounced, so words starting with it begin directly on the following vowel sound.

endings.title: Rule endings
endings.note: Underlined endings in the forms and this table come from the same rule. A dash marks a person not used in that tense.

present.name: Present
present.use: Use it for actions happening now, general truths, and regular habits.
present.form: Add the tense endings to the verb stem, such as -e, -es, -e, -ons, -ez, -ent for regular -er verbs.

passeCompose.name: Passé composé
passeCompose.use: Use it for completed actions and specific events in the past.
passeCompose.form: Combine the present tense of avoir or être with the past participle.

imparfait.name: Imparfait
imparfait.use: Use it for ongoing background situations, descriptions, and repeated habits in the past.
imparfait.form: Take the present indicative nous form, remove -ons, and add -ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient. Être uses ét-.

plusQueParfait.name: Plus-que-parfait
plusQueParfait.use: Use it for an action that was already completed before another past action or moment.
plusQueParfait.form: Combine the imparfait of avoir or être with the past participle.

futur.name: Future
futur.use: Use it for actions or events that will happen in the future.
futur.form: For regular verbs, use the infinitive (dropping the final -e of -re verbs) and add -ai, -as, -a, -ons, -ez, -ont.

futurAnterieur.name: Futur antérieur
futurAnterieur.use: Use it for an action that will already be completed before a future moment.
futurAnterieur.form: Combine the futur of avoir or être with the past participle.

conditionnel.name: Conditional
conditionnel.use: Use it for polite requests, wishes, hypothetical situations, and advice.
conditionnel.form: Add the imparfait endings -ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient to the future stem.

conditionnelPasse.name: Conditionnel passé
conditionnelPasse.use: Use it for a past hypothesis, a regret, or a reproach about what did not happen.
conditionnelPasse.form: Combine the conditionnel of avoir or être with the past participle.

subjonctif.name: Subjunctive
subjonctif.use: Some expressions of necessity, doubt, emotion, wishes or subjective evaluation introduce a clause in the subjunctive. The expression and context determine the mood.
subjonctif.form: Usually introduced by que. Most verbs take -e, -es, -e, -ions, -iez, -ent; the stem may differ by person. Some verbs have irregular forms, such as que je sois and que j’aie.

subjonctifPasse.name: Subjonctif passé
subjonctifPasse.use: Use it in a clause requiring the subjunctive when the action is viewed as completed before the relevant reference point, which may be past, present or future.
subjonctifPasse.form: Usually introduced by que. Combine the present subjunctive of avoir or être with the past participle.

imperatif.name: Imperative
imperatif.use: Use it to give direct orders, advice, instructions, or prohibitions.
imperatif.form: Usually use the present indicative tu, nous and vous forms without subject pronouns. The tu forms of -er verbs, aller and verbs like ouvrir have no final -s (parle, va, ouvre), but take -s before directly attached y or en (vas-y, parles-en). Être, avoir, savoir and vouloir have special imperative forms.

rules.er-regular: Standard -er verbs keep an unchanged stem throughout all tenses, as in nous parlons.
rules.er-cer: Verbs ending in -cer change c to ç before a and o to keep the soft sound, as in nous commençons.
rules.er-ger: Verbs ending in -ger insert a silent e after g before a and o to keep the soft sound, as in nous mangeons.
rules.er-yer-i: In -oyer and -uyer verbs, y becomes i before a silent e (ils nettoient, ils essuient). Verbs in -ayer allow y or i; -eyer keeps y. Envoyer and renvoyer have irregular future and conditional stems.
rules.er-e-grave: In verbs following the lever pattern, the stem’s mute e becomes è before a syllable containing mute e, including in the future and conditional (il lève, il lèvera).
rules.er-eacute-egrave: In verbs following the préférer pattern, stem é becomes è before a syllable containing mute e (je préfère). Future and conditional spellings may be traditional (je préférerai, je préférerais) or rectified (je préfèrerai, je préfèrerais).
rules.er-eler-double: Doubling verbs in -eler and -eter double l or t before a silent syllable and throughout the future and conditional, as in j’appelle.
rules.ir-issons: Regular second-group -ir verbs use -iss- in the plural present indicative, throughout the imparfait and present subjunctive, and in the present participle (nous choisissons).
rules.ir-sortir: Verbs like sortir and partir drop the stem’s final consonant in the singular present, as in je sors.
rules.ir-ouvrir: Verbs like ouvrir and offrir take standard -er verb endings in the present tense, as in j’ouvre.
rules.re-regular: Regular -dre verbs like vendre take -s, -s, and no ending in the singular present, as in il vend.
